phaseCues.intro: This is the briefing. You will meet the person on trial and learn the charge. Listen for what the prosecution must prove — you decide later if they proved it.
phaseCues.openings: Now you will hear openings. Each side tells its story of the case before any evidence is called. Notice what each side asks you to believe.
phaseCues.beats: Now the evidence. Witnesses and exhibits come one at a time. You do not decide yet — just listen carefully.
phaseCues.closings: Now the closings. Each side makes its final argument. After this, you retire with the jury to deliberate — you lock your own position only after that discussion.
phaseCues.verdict: If, after considering all the evidence, you are not sure the prosecution proved every element beyond reasonable doubt, your verdict must be Not Guilty.
phaseCues.juryroom: Welcome to the jury room. Under the fictional Aster Reach procedure used here, all 12 jurors first try to agree after three focused rounds. You may pause, reopen written notes, or raise a point. Then choose a verdict or remain undecided. If the first ballot is not unanimous, the judge gives a neutral direction: keep considering each view without surrendering an honestly held one. Eleven matching votes can then return a verdict; undecided jurors remain undecided and may leave the jury hung.
phaseCues.reveal: This is the post-verdict review. Compare your reasoning with the authors’ reference verdict and the evidence they gave greatest weight. It is an editorial view, not a score.

direction: {name}, {role}, now gives the legal direction. Keep each element separate as you listen.
The legal rules now come from {name}, {role}. This is law, not evidence.
{name}, {role}, returns to the rules that bind your decision. Notice what cannot substitute for proof.
exhibit: {name} presents the next exhibit. Separate the record itself from the inference counsel asks you to draw.
An exhibit is now shown through {name}. Ask where it came from, what it establishes, and where its limits begin.
{name} turns to a document or physical item. Notice its source, custody, and what it cannot identify by itself.
cross: Cross-examination of {name} now begins. Listen for a real concession, not merely agreed wording.
Cross-examination of {name} tests the account. Notice whether the answer accepts the premise, qualifies it, or resists it.
Cross-examination of {name} begins. Short propositions will test memory, method, and limits.
prosecution: The prosecution calls {name}, {role}. Keep direct recollection separate from reconstruction or assumption.
{name}, {role}, now gives evidence for the prosecution. Note both the point and its limits.
{name}, {role}, is called for the prosecution. Listen for what they personally saw, did, or authenticated.
defence: The defence calls {name}, {role}. Listen for the competing account and the evidence that supports it.
{name}, {role}, now gives evidence for the defence. Test it by the same standard as every other witness.
{name}, {role}, is called for the defence. Notice whether the evidence exposes a gap or offers a different inference.
